title: Selection and Aggregation in Forecasting
hook: The average of five independent estimates is almost always more accurate than the estimate five people agree on after discussion.
counterintuition: Group involvement improves most things. But in estimation, group discussion does something specific: it replaces independent variation in each person's estimate with social influence. Estimates converge not because information flowed but because people adjusted toward whoever spoke first or most confidently. What emerges is not the group's combined knowledge. It is the first speaker's estimate, softened by politeness.
tryThisNow: Before your next group estimation, ask everyone to write their number before anyone speaks. Collect the papers and calculate the mean. Put that mean on the board before discussion begins. Notice what changes.
keyTakeaway: Independent estimates aggregated outperform the same estimates collapsed by discussion. The aggregation advantage requires one condition: inputs must be genuinely independent before combination. Discussion removes that condition.

breakdown.fastRead:
Give eight analysts identical information and ask each to produce an independent price forecast. Then ask all eight to meet and produce a committee consensus. Compare the two methods across many trials. The aggregated independent forecasts will almost always be more accurate.

The committee is not less expert. Its discussion adds noise through convergence: as the group talks, estimates move toward whoever spoke first and most confidently. The late speakers' independent estimates disappear into their decision to agree. The aggregated forecast captured all eight estimates before any adjustment. The committee consensus captured one estimate spread across eight faces.
breakdown.deepRead:
Ask a group of experienced forecasters to estimate the probability of a geopolitical event. Do this twice: once with independent written submissions before any discussion, and once with the group discussing and then converging on a number. Average the pre-discussion estimates. Compare that average against the consensus that emerged from discussion. Across many such trials, the pre-discussion average will track outcomes more accurately.

Consider what happens when eight people each hold a slightly different probability estimate for the same event. One person has noticed a factor others overlooked. Another has weighted base rates more carefully. A third has built a model from a different set of historical analogues. Each estimate encodes a distinct piece of information. When those eight people discuss, the person who speaks first sets a reference point, and the others adjust toward or away from it rather than averaging across their independent analyses. The final consensus is not an average. It is a trajectory from the first speaker's position, modified by social dynamics. Research on independent forecast aggregation shows the advantage is consistent across many domains: commodity prices, geopolitical events, clinical outcomes, sports results. The wisdom of crowds works when the crowd's members have not been talking to each other. The moment the group discusses, the wisdom becomes the loudest voice, and the crowd becomes an echo.

Aggregation and discussion are not alternatives in a spectrum of group involvement. They are different operations acting on different things: aggregation operates on information; discussion operates on people.

The average of a post-discussion consensus is the average of a social convergence process, not the average of eight minds.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 3:00 on a Thursday, Eugene pulls the 12-quarter tracking error chart from his desk drawer and spreads it next to the meeting notes from this quarter's analyst review session. The chart compares two forecasting methods for quarterly commodity prices. Left column: pre-meeting aggregated analyst estimates, submitted individually before the Monday review call. Right column: committee consensus produced at the end of that call. Over 12 quarters, the aggregated column tracks actuals more closely. The gap is 30 percent in tracking error. The analysts who attended those meetings are excellent forecasters. Six of eight adjusted their estimates toward whoever spoke first on the Monday call. The pre-meeting submission procedure captures the version of each analyst's estimate that existed before that adjustment.

Decades of research across forecasting competitions have produced a consistent finding: combining independent probability estimates from a diverse pool outperforms both individual expert estimates and group deliberation, and the advantage appears across commodity markets, geopolitical events, sports results, and medical outcomes. The advantage is not trivial: well-designed aggregation often outperforms the best individual forecaster in the pool, and the gap over group deliberation is larger still. Aggregation preserves the information that individual estimates encode; group deliberation replaces that information with a social convergence process.

'Why do we even have a joint planning call if the independent submissions are more accurate?' Otto's question to his regional managers is not rhetorical. He has the forecast error reports in front of him: 14 percent mean absolute error in the independent-submission cycle, 19 percent in the joint-planning-call cycle. The call transcripts show why: three managers adjusted their estimates toward the most senior manager who spoke first, pulling the regional average in a direction the data did not support. Otto's proposed fix is not to eliminate the call. It is to collect all submitted forecasts before the call begins, calculate the aggregate, and put that number on screen before anyone speaks. The call becomes a residual check, not a convergence session.

Rosalind presents the question to the investment committee before opening the historical data. If the associates submitted independent exit probability estimates for the same portfolio companies before last year's committee meetings, and you aggregated those estimates, were they more or less accurate than the probabilities the committee converged on in the meeting? The room resists: it sounds like a challenge to the partners' judgment. Rosalind reframes it as a question about what happens when the room's optimism pulls all estimates above the aggregated pre-meeting mean. The historical data shows the aggregated associate mean was more accurate. The partners' optimism in the room was a bias; the aggregation had already averaged it away.

When you collect pre-meeting estimates, you are doing something structurally different from running a poll. The poll asks for opinion after discussion. The pre-meeting collection asks for analysis before influence. What each person submits reflects their own information, weighting, and model. The aggregate of those submissions does not merely average opinions. It combines independent analyses that have not yet been modified by social pressure to agree. That is what makes the aggregate more than the mean of the post-discussion estimates: the post-discussion estimates are not independent anymore.

Selection still matters: an aggregate of poorly calibrated inputs will be poorly calibrated. But for a given pool, the aggregate of independent submissions outperforms the same pool's post-discussion consensus. The independence is the condition that makes combination worth doing.

memorableLines.text: The aggregated forecast captured all eight estimates before any adjustment. The committee consensus captured one estimate spread across eight faces.
memorableLines.why: The parallel structure makes the contrast between aggregation and consensus precise: one preserves eight independent signals; the other distributes one anchored signal across eight people.

memorableLines.text: The wisdom of crowds works when the crowd's members have not been talking to each other. The moment the group discusses, the wisdom becomes the loudest voice, and the crowd becomes an echo.
memorableLines.why: Names the exact condition under which the crowds benefit operates and the exact mechanism through which discussion destroys it, in two sentences with matching parallel structure.

memorableLines.text: The aggregate of those submissions does not merely average opinions. It combines independent analyses that have not yet been modified by social pressure to agree.
memorableLines.why: Draws the sharpest line between averaging and aggregating: averaging operates on outputs after social modification; true aggregation combines inputs before modification.

examples.title: Six of Eight

planSpec.domain: commodity price forecasting: a trading firm comparing aggregated analyst forecasts versus committee consensus on quarterly oil price
planSpec.audience: a trading desk manager studying whether analyst meetings before forecast submission harm accuracy
planSpec.stakes: hedging decisions worth tens of millions — the difference between aggregated and committee consensus translates directly into position sizing error
planSpec.requiredBeat: the desk manager compares 12-quarter tracking error: pre-meeting aggregated individual estimates have 30 percent lower tracking error than post-meeting committee consensus, and a post-meeting survey shows 6 of 8 analysts adjusted their estimates toward the person who spoke first

examples.scenario: At 3:00 on a Thursday, Eugene spreads the 12-quarter tracking error chart next to the meeting notes from this quarter's analyst review session. Two forecast method columns: pre-meeting aggregated individual estimates and post-meeting committee consensus. Over 12 quarters, the aggregated column tracks actuals 30 percent more closely. A post-meeting survey answers why: 6 of 8 analysts adjusted their estimate toward whoever spoke first. The information each analyst held independently survived until Monday morning. The meeting compressed it to a social average.
examples.whatToDo: Require analyst forecast submissions before any group review session. Aggregate the submissions and bring the aggregate to the meeting as the starting point, not as a result to be overridden.
examples.whyItMatters: Pre-meeting submission captures each analyst's independent estimate before the meeting's social dynamics compress the distribution. The 30 percent tracking error reduction is the size of what the meeting was destroying.

examples.title: 28 of 40

planSpec.domain: geopolitical event probability forecasting: an intelligence assessment team comparing aggregated analyst estimates versus a roundtable consensus
planSpec.audience: an intelligence unit quality officer comparing two assessment methods for the same event across a historical set
planSpec.stakes: policy decisions based on probability estimates — systematically anchored estimates lead to policy options being mispriced
planSpec.requiredBeat: the quality officer analyzes historical data across 40 geopolitical events: aggregated individual estimates were better calibrated than roundtable consensus estimates in 28 of 40 cases; in the 12 cases where consensus was better, the margin was smaller than in the 28 where aggregation was better

examples.scenario: Muriel reviews forty events where both methods produced estimates. In 28 of 40 cases, the aggregated individual estimates were better calibrated against outcomes than the roundtable consensus. In the 12 cases where roundtable was better, the margin of advantage was smaller than in the 28 cases where aggregation won. The calibration chart separates the two methods clearly: the roundtable curve drifts away from the diagonal in the high-probability range, the direction senior voices tend to push estimates. The aggregated curve holds closer throughout.
examples.whatToDo: For recurring high-stakes probability estimates, track both methods against outcomes over time. When aggregation outperforms consensus in both win rate and margin, restructure the process to aggregate independent submissions rather than produce roundtable consensus.
examples.whyItMatters: The 28-of-40 advantage with larger margins in the aggregation wins shows a consistent directional bias in roundtable consensus: senior or first voices pull estimates away from the distribution that independent analysis would produce.

examples.title: 14 vs. 19

planSpec.domain: product demand forecasting: a consumer goods company comparing sales forecast accuracy when regional managers submit independently versus after a joint planning call
planSpec.audience: a supply chain planning director who has run both methods across consecutive forecast cycles
planSpec.stakes: inventory levels and customer service rates — over- or under-production driven by poor forecasts directly affects cash flow and fill rates
planSpec.requiredBeat: the planning director and a regional manager compare forecast error rates: independent-submission cycle had 14 percent MAPE; joint-planning-call cycle had 19 percent; transcript analysis shows estimates clustered toward the first regional manager who spoke

examples.scenario: 'Why do we even have the call if the independent submissions are more accurate?' Otto slides both error reports across the table to his regional manager. Independent-submission cycle: 14 percent mean absolute error. Joint-planning-call cycle: 19 percent. The call transcripts explain the gap: three managers adjusted their estimates toward the most senior manager who spoke first, pulling the regional average away from the data. 'The call is useful,' Otto says. 'It should start with the aggregated forecast on screen, not with each region's first impression of the quarter.'
examples.whatToDo: Collect all forecast submissions before any joint session begins. Calculate the aggregate and display it before the session opens. Use the session to investigate deviations from the aggregate, not to produce a new consensus from scratch.
examples.whyItMatters: The 5-percentage-point error increase in the joint-call cycle, traced to clustering around the first speaker, shows that the call's social dynamics were replacing independent analysis rather than combining it.

examples.title: More Accurate

planSpec.domain: startup exit probability forecasting: a venture capital firm comparing aggregated associate estimates versus partner committee vote on portfolio company exit probability
planSpec.audience: a VC firm investment committee advisor comparing both methods' historical accuracy
planSpec.stakes: portfolio valuation and fund return projections — systematically optimistic committee estimates lead to fund return misrepresentation
planSpec.requiredBeat: the advisor asks the partners whether their associates' aggregated pre-meeting exit probability estimates were more or less accurate than the committee consensus; historical data shows aggregated associate mean was more accurate; partner optimism in the meeting consistently pulled the committee above the aggregated mean

examples.scenario: Before opening the historical data, Rosalind poses the question to the partners: when associates submitted independent exit probability estimates before last year's committee meetings, and you aggregated those estimates, were they more or less accurate than the probabilities you converged on in the meeting? The room resists. Rosalind reframes it: this is not about competence. It is about what the room's optimism does to the distribution. The historical data shows the aggregated associate mean tracked outcomes more closely. The committee consensus ran consistently above it. The meeting did not combine information. It adjusted the aggregate upward by mood.
examples.whatToDo: Before any committee valuation or probability discussion, collect and aggregate independent estimates from all contributors. Present the aggregate as the opening anchor. Track whether committee deliberation consistently moves the aggregate in one direction, and investigate whether that direction matches outcomes.
examples.whyItMatters: When committee consensus consistently exceeds the aggregated pre-meeting mean, and the mean tracks outcomes better, the committee's deliberation is introducing a directional bias rather than improving on the aggregation.

examples.title: 0.72 vs. 0.58

planSpec.domain: clinical trial outcome probability: a pharmaceutical team comparing aggregated investigator estimates versus a steering committee consensus on trial success probability
planSpec.audience: a clinical development program manager comparing two probability-elicitation methods for the same historical trial set
planSpec.stakes: go/no-go investment decisions — overconfident committee consensus probabilities lead to under-resourced contingency planning
planSpec.requiredBeat: you introduce a protocol requiring investigators to submit individual probability estimates before each steering committee meeting; six months in, aggregated pre-meeting estimates correlate 0.72 with actual outcomes versus 0.58 for committee consensus estimates

examples.scenario: You introduce a protocol requiring each investigator to submit an individual trial success probability before the steering committee meeting. Six months in, you pull the comparison data: aggregated pre-meeting estimates correlate 0.72 with actual trial outcomes; committee consensus estimates for the same trials correlate 0.58. Both sets used the same information. The difference is that the aggregated estimates were formed independently, before the committee's discussion anchored the more optimistic investigators' views toward the consensus. You route the six-month comparison to the program director before the next protocol review.
examples.whatToDo: Require individual probability submissions before every steering committee meeting and track the aggregate separately from the committee consensus. When the aggregate consistently outperforms the consensus, the pre-submission protocol is the process to protect.
examples.whyItMatters: A 0.14-point correlation gap between independent aggregation and committee consensus, across the same trials and same information, shows that the committee's discussion is reducing forecast accuracy rather than improving it.

examples.title: What the Review Replaced

planSpec.domain: championship prediction: a sports analytics team comparing aggregated analyst probability estimates versus editorial committee consensus before a tournament
planSpec.audience: a sports analytics platform manager studying whether pre-publication editorial review distorts aggregated model outputs
planSpec.stakes: platform credibility — if editorial review adjusts aggregated outputs toward popular favorites, the platform's advertised independence is compromised
planSpec.requiredBeat: the platform manager reviews three years of pre-tournament predictions: aggregated analyst estimates had a Brier score of 0.21; post-editorial-review published estimates had a Brier score of 0.24; editorial review consistently moved predictions toward teams with large fan bases

examples.scenario: The platform's prediction archive spreads across Adelaide's desk: three years of pre-tournament win probabilities, two columns for each event. Aggregated analyst estimates: Brier score 0.21. Post-editorial-review published estimates: 0.24. Manual comparison of the divergences shows a pattern: editorial review moved predictions toward teams with large fan bases in eight of twelve cases examined. The analytical aggregation was replaced with audience-serving selection before publication. The aggregated column would have been better. What reached users was the editorial judgment of what users wanted to believe.
examples.whatToDo: Treat editorial review of aggregated outputs as a potential noise introduction step. Track Brier scores or equivalent accuracy measures for both the aggregated inputs and the published outputs. If published outputs consistently underperform the aggregated inputs, the review process is reducing accuracy, not improving it.
examples.whyItMatters: A Brier score of 0.24 versus 0.21 after editorial review, with divergences consistently toward popular favorites, shows that the review replaced analytical aggregation with audience preference. The aggregation's accuracy advantage was destroyed by the review step.

questions.prompt: What is the key mechanism through which aggregating independent forecasts outperforms group deliberation?
choices: The aggregated pool contains more forecasters, whose individual accuracy averages to a higher level than any single expert.
Aggregation allows the group to consider more options simultaneously rather than narrowing to a single position.
Aggregation preserves the independent information each estimate encodes; group deliberation replaces that information with social influence and convergence toward an anchor.
questions.explanation: The key word is independence. Each forecaster's estimate contains information shaped by their particular analysis. Aggregation combines those pieces. Discussion causes them to converge on a social reference point before the combination can occur.

questions.prompt: A trading desk manager finds that pre-meeting aggregated analyst estimates produce 30 percent lower tracking error than post-meeting committee consensus over 12 quarters. A post-meeting survey shows 6 of 8 analysts adjusted toward whoever spoke first. What is the most direct explanation for the tracking-error difference?
choices: The individual estimates are submitted by analysts who have more domain expertise than those who dominate the committee discussion.

The committee consensus is anchored to the first analyst who speaks, which compresses the distribution of estimates toward a single social reference point and discards the independent information in the other estimates.
Individual estimates submitted before the meeting are more carefully reasoned because there is no social pressure during the submission process.
questions.explanation: The 6-of-8 survey result directly shows the anchoring mechanism: most analysts adjusted toward the first speaker. The committee consensus is not an average of eight independent analyses. It is the first speaker's estimate, modified by social interaction.

questions.prompt: A supply chain planning director compares two forecast cycles: independent-submission mean absolute error was 14 percent; joint-planning-call mean absolute error was 19 percent. Call transcripts show estimates clustered toward the first speaker. What does this pattern reveal?
choices: The joint planning call did not combine the regional managers' independent information. It replaced that information with a social convergence process anchored to the first speaker.
The independent-submission cycle used a different set of managers who happened to produce more accurate forecasts.
The planning call introduced new information that increased complexity, which paradoxically reduced accuracy through information overload.
questions.explanation: Transcript evidence of clustering toward the first speaker shows the call produced social convergence, not information combination. The 5-percentage-point accuracy gap is the cost of replacing the independent estimates with a discussion-anchored consensus.

questions.prompt: You introduce a protocol requiring pharmaceutical steering committee members to submit individual trial success probabilities before each meeting. Six months in, aggregated pre-meeting estimates correlate 0.72 with actual outcomes versus 0.58 for committee consensus. Which action most directly preserves this advantage?
choices: Require committee members to provide written rationales with their probability estimates to improve the quality of each individual input.
Continue collecting individual estimates before any meeting discussion and aggregate them as the starting point, maintaining independence before combination.
Select committee members with stronger track records in probability estimation to improve the quality of the pool.
questions.explanation: The advantage comes from independence before aggregation. Continuing to collect submissions before discussion is what preserves independence. Adding rationales and selecting members may improve input quality but do not directly protect the structural condition that produced the advantage.

questions.prompt: A sports analytics platform's aggregated analyst estimates (Brier score 0.21) outperform post-editorial-review published estimates (Brier score 0.24). The adjustments in editorial review consistently moved predictions toward popular teams. What does the Brier score comparison reveal?
choices: The editorial review process replaced analytical aggregation with audience preference, introducing a systematic bias that made the published estimates less accurate than the aggregated ones.
The aggregated estimates were produced by a larger pool with more diverse analytical methods, which automatically produced better Brier scores than any single editorial judgment could.
Editorial review added contextual information about team popularity that the aggregated model underweighted, but the model's simplicity outperformed the richer editorial analysis by chance.
questions.explanation: The directional pattern of adjustments toward popular teams, combined with the accuracy decrease, identifies the mechanism: editorial review was not adding information. It was substituting audience preference for analytical output, which degraded accuracy.

questions.prompt: A forecasting team proposes improving their process by asking each forecaster to share a rationale before submitting their estimate, so the group can benefit from each person's reasoning before providing a number. Does this preserve the independence of forecasts?
choices: Yes, because the rationales help less-experienced forecasters apply their knowledge more effectively, improving the quality of the inputs before aggregation.
Yes, because sharing reasoning is informational rather than social: rationales are different from anchoring on a specific number.
No, because sharing rationales before submission allows early rationales to anchor the analytical framing for later submitters, which reduces the independence of the inputs before they are combined.
questions.explanation: Independence is violated before a number is offered. Early rationales shape the analytical framing of later submitters just as early numbers anchor their estimates. The mechanism of social influence operates on framing and reasoning, not only on explicit numeric anchors.

questions.prompt: An investment firm wants to improve the accuracy of portfolio company exit probability estimates. Which process change most directly applies the selection-and-aggregation principle?
choices: Replace the partner committee with a single highly experienced analyst whose individual forecasts have historically outperformed the committee.
Collect independent exit probability estimates from all analysts and associates before any partner review meeting, and aggregate those estimates as the baseline before the committee deliberates.
Require the committee to produce three alternative probability scenarios rather than a single estimate, to capture more of the outcome space.
questions.explanation: Selection-and-aggregation means: choose who is in the pool, then collect and combine their independent estimates before social influence can modify them. Aggregating before the committee deliberates is the direct application of the principle.

questions.prompt: You are designing a group estimation process for a project planning session. Which design most directly preserves the conditions for aggregation to work?
choices: Ask each team member to submit their estimate privately and then discuss the range to understand sources of disagreement before finalizing.
Use the median of the team's estimates as the official forecast to reduce the influence of outliers on the final number.
Require each team member to write and submit their estimate before anyone shares their number, then calculate the mean before any discussion begins.
questions.explanation: The mean calculated before anyone shares their number is the aggregation of independent inputs. Discussing after submission is fine, but the aggregate calculated before discussion is the measure to anchor. Revealing estimates to discuss them before the aggregate is calculated reintroduces social influence.

questions.prompt: After introducing a pre-meeting submission requirement, a manager notices that team members have started discussing the project informally in smaller groups before the meeting. If those conversations are happening, does the pre-meeting submission requirement still preserve the conditions for aggregation to work?
choices: No, because the pre-meeting conversations mean submitted estimates are no longer independent; some have already been influenced by others before submission, which undermines the aggregation advantage.
Yes, because the formal submission requirement ensures each person writes their own estimate, which prevents the specific anchoring effect that occurs during open deliberation.
Yes, because informal conversations are less influential than structured deliberation, so the independence of estimates is sufficiently preserved for aggregation to still outperform consensus.
questions.explanation: Independence is a structural condition, not a procedural one. Pre-meeting informal discussions violate independence before submission. The formal submission requirement only captures what was already influenced. The aggregation advantage requires that submissions be genuinely independent, not merely written independently.

reviewCards.front: Why does aggregating independent forecasts outperform group deliberation?
reviewCards.back: Each independent estimate contains information shaped by that person's unique analysis. Aggregation combines those distinct inputs. Group deliberation causes estimates to converge toward whoever spoke first, replacing information combination with social influence.

reviewCards.front: What condition must hold for aggregation to improve on individual judgment?
reviewCards.back: The inputs must be genuinely independent before they are combined. If forecasters have already discussed with each other, shared rationales, or been exposed to early estimates, their submissions are no longer independent and the aggregation advantage is reduced or eliminated.

reviewCards.front: What is the anchoring effect in group forecast deliberation?
reviewCards.back: When a group discusses a forecast openly, the first specific number or position offered becomes a reference point. Subsequent contributors adjust toward or away from it rather than averaging their independent analyses. The final consensus reflects the first speaker's position more than the group's combined information.

reviewCards.front: How does the pre-meeting submission protocol preserve aggregation's advantage?
reviewCards.back: It requires each contributor to commit their estimate before any social reference point exists. The submitted estimates capture independent analyses formed without exposure to the group. Aggregating those estimates before discussion combines information rather than social convergence.

reviewCards.front: Why does selection still matter in aggregation?
reviewCards.back: Aggregation averages inputs: if all inputs share the same systematic bias, the aggregate inherits that bias. The pool's composition determines whether diverse information sources are included. A well-aggregated pool of poorly calibrated forecasters produces a well-aggregated poor forecast.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Design forecasting and estimation processes to collect independent inputs before any social interaction, then aggregate those inputs before deliberation begins. The two-step design is: (1) collect all submissions with no sharing between contributors, and (2) bring the aggregate to the group as the starting point. Deliberation after the aggregate is formed serves to investigate residuals and outliers, not to produce a new number from social convergence.

ifThenPlans.context: You are running a regular forecasting or estimation session where a group meets to produce a consensus number.
ifThenPlans.plan: Require all participants to submit their individual estimates in writing before the meeting begins, with no visibility into others' submissions. Calculate the aggregate before the meeting opens. Display the aggregate as the opening data point. Use the meeting to discuss the largest deviations from the aggregate and their sources, not to produce a new consensus number from scratch.

ifThenPlans.context: You discover that the consensus your group produces in meetings consistently outperforms or underperforms the aggregated pre-meeting submissions in a particular direction.
ifThenPlans.plan: The directional pattern identifies a systematic bias that the deliberation is introducing. If the meeting consistently produces numbers above the aggregated mean, the meeting's social dynamics are pulling estimates upward. Name the source of the pull (seniority, optimism, audience preference) and restructure the meeting so the aggregate holds as the anchor rather than as one input among many.

ifThenPlans.context: You want to know whether your group's deliberation process is combining information or producing social convergence.
ifThenPlans.plan: Run a comparison over 10 or more cases: compare the accuracy of the pre-meeting aggregated submissions against the final post-deliberation consensus for the same cases. If the aggregate consistently outperforms the consensus, the deliberation is introducing noise. If performance is roughly equal, the deliberation may be adding genuine information from discussion. Track the margin and direction of any consistent gap.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, identify one upcoming meeting where your group will estimate a number or probability together. Before the meeting, send a brief form asking each person to write their estimate. Collect all responses before anyone shares theirs. Calculate the mean. Open the meeting with that mean on the board. Watch what the conversation changes when an aggregate anchors the room instead of the first speaker.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, for any meeting where your group produced a consensus estimate, record both the consensus and the individual estimates submitted before discussion. After the outcome is known, check which was more accurate. After four weeks, you will know whether your deliberation process is adding or removing accuracy from your group's combined knowledge.
